notes.meaning: During the Passover meal, Jesus took bread, thanked God, broke it into pieces, and gave it to His followers. He told them to eat it because it represented His body, which was about to be sacrificed on the cross. By doing this, He gave the ancient Passover meal a new meaning that points to Himself.

differ.view: Christ's true physical body is present in, with, and under the bread and wine during the sacrament.
Christ is spiritually present to the believer's faith, feeding the soul through the Holy Spirit rather than physically in the elements.
The bread is a memorial symbol that helps believers remember Christ's body given on the cross.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The bread changes completely into the actual physical body of Christ, leaving only the outward appearance of bread.

notes.meaning: Next, Jesus took a cup of wine, gave thanks to God, and handed it to the disciples. He told all of them to drink from it together. Sharing this cup showed that every follower has a part in the blessings He was about to provide.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The whole Christ is fully present in each element, so church members receive all the spiritual blessings of the sacrament even when receiving only the bread.

notes.meaning: Jesus explained that the wine pointed to His own blood, which would soon be poured out in death. This blood established a new covenant, which is a sacred agreement and promise of salvation between God and humanity. His sacrifice makes complete forgiveness of sins possible for everyone who trusts in Him.

Jesus told His disciples that He would not drink wine again until the day He drinks it anew with them in His Father's kingdom. His earthly fellowship at the Passover table was coming to an end with His approaching death. This statement gave them hope by pointing forward to a joyful future feast together in heaven.

Before leaving the room, Jesus and His disciples sang a hymn of praise together, following the Passover custom of singing Psalms. Then they walked out of Jerusalem toward the Mount of Olives. Even with terrible suffering waiting for Him, Jesus faced the night with praise to God.

On the way, Jesus warned the disciples that every one of them would abandon Him that very night. He quoted the ancient prophet Zechariah, who wrote that God's Shepherd would be struck down and the sheep would be scattered. Hard times were coming, but this painful trial was fulfilling God's plan.

Jesus immediately gave them comfort by promising that He would rise from the dead. Like a caring shepherd, He promised to go ahead of them into Galilee to gather them back together. Even though they would fail Him, His love and commitment to them would not end.

Peter boldly replied that even if all the other disciples fell away, he never would. He truly loved Jesus, but he trusted too much in his own strength and did not recognize his own weakness. Overconfidence often leaves a person unprepared for sudden temptation.

Jesus answered Peter with a solemn truth about what would happen before morning. He told Peter that before the rooster crowed to announce the dawn, he would deny knowing Jesus three separate times. Jesus knew Peter's heart and weaknesses far better than Peter did.

Peter insisted even more strongly that he would rather die with Jesus than deny Him. All the other disciples made the very same promise. They all meant well, but human courage quickly melts when real danger arrives.

Jesus brought the disciples to an olive orchard called Gethsemane, located near the Mount of Olives. He instructed most of the group to sit down while He walked a little farther to pray. He regularly went to this quiet spot, and He entered it willingly even though He knew He would be arrested there.

Jesus invited His three closest disciples, Peter, James, and John, to come deeper into the garden with Him. There, an overwhelming sorrow and deep distress began to press upon His soul. The same men who had seen His heavenly glory on the mountain were now invited to witness His deepest anguish.

Jesus told the three disciples that His grief was so crushing it felt like dying. He asked them to stay awake, keep watch, and share in His sorrow. As a true human being, Jesus deeply desired comfort and companionship from His friends during this dark hour.

Walking a short distance farther, Jesus bowed with His face touching the ground and cried out to God. He asked if there was any possible way for this bitter cup of suffering and divine judgment for sin to pass from Him. Yet He immediately yielded His human desires completely to the Father's will.

Returning to the three disciples, Jesus found them sound asleep instead of praying. He spoke directly to Peter, asking if they were unable to stay awake with Him for even a single hour. Peter had just promised to die for Him, yet he could not even stay awake to support Him.

Jesus urged them to stay alert and pray so they would not fall into temptation when the testing began. He explained that a person's inner spirit may want to do right, but human physical nature is weak and easily fails. Prayer is essential because our best intentions cannot stand without God's strength.

Jesus stepped away a second time to pour out His heart to God. This time He accepted that the cup could not pass away if people were to be saved, and He prayed, 'May Your will be done.' In this agonizing moment, He showed perfect obedience to the Father's plan of redemption.

When Jesus walked back to the disciples again, He found them sleeping once more because their eyes were so heavy. Emotional sorrow and late-night exhaustion had completely overpowered them. Even in the midst of extreme danger, human weakness pulled them back to sleep.

Jesus left them sleeping and went away to pray a third time, repeating the very same words. Repeating the same prayer showed the great depth of His anguish, not empty routine. True earnestness before God often repeats a desperate plea until peace is found.

Returning to His followers a final time, Jesus told them their time for resting was over. The critical moment had arrived, and the Son of Man was about to be handed over to sinful men. The inward struggle of prayer was finished, and the outward trial was now beginning.

Jesus told His disciples to get up and go with Him to meet what was coming. He announced that the man who was betraying Him had already arrived nearby. Instead of running away to save Himself, Jesus stepped forward willingly to face His enemies.

Before Jesus finished speaking, Judas, one of the twelve chosen disciples, stepped into view. A large mob armed with swords and wooden clubs came with him, sent by the Jewish religious leaders. The scene was shocking because someone from Jesus' inner circle was now leading an armed crowd to capture Him.

Judas had given the armed men a prearranged sign so they would know which person to seize in the dark. He told them to arrest whichever man he kissed. What was normally a warm sign of love and honor was turned into a cold tool of betrayal.

Judas walked straight up to Jesus, greeted Him as 'Rabbi,' and kissed Him warmly. He acted like a devoted student greeting a loved teacher, hiding his evil purpose behind friendly words. False friendship can often disguise the deepest hostility.

Jesus answered Judas by calling him 'Friend' and telling him to do what he had come to do. Then the soldiers moved in, grabbed Jesus, and placed Him under arrest. Even while being handed over to death, Jesus treated His betrayer with calm dignity and surrendered by His own choice.
